messages.author: 5900eadecec2d82d
messages.subject: Re: zero values analyzed as 4th species
parts: Hi Genisis,

> >1.) In my observation layer, I am post stratifying by species. I am
> >including line transect censuses that did not have any sightings.
> >Distance is treating these no sightings (no matter if they are entered
> >as "0" or "default") as a fourth species, and I am afraid this is
> >biasing my results. How can I tell Distance not to analyze zero values
> >as a forth species?

Line transects that did not have any sightings should not have any records in
the Observation layer. They should not be "0" or "default". For an example,
see the online help, Users Guide page "Data in Distance - Data Structure".
There is a picture there of a data sheet (3rd picture down), in which there
are no observations for line transect numbers 9, 10, 11, 12.

If this still doesn't make sense to you, and you have read the Users Guide
carefully from cover to cover, then please send me a copy of your distance
project file, zipped up and I will edit it to show you what I mean. (please
send to me privately: dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk , not to the list.)

> >2.) Results are showing that my f(0), p, and ESW is exactly the same for
> >all three species, including my zero values (the imaginary fourth
> >species). Why is this happening, and how can I fix it?

You need to estimate the detection function by stratum. You do this in the
Model Definition, Estimate tab - there is a box half way down where you can
check the "Detection Function" line, "Stratum" column. See online help page
"Model Definition Properties - Estiamte"

> >3.) Also, although this question may arise more from my ignorance than
> >anything else, how can I have a detection probability greater than 1, or
> >100%? The first histogram bar on Plot three rises to a detection
> >probability of 1.54. Do I ignore that and just look at my red function
> >line (which does rise to exactly 1)?

Yes, the labelling on this graph is a bit confusing. The line shows the
estimated detection probability (which is 1 at disance = 0), while the
histograms are the frequency that objects are observed in each band, scaled
so that the observed number is equal to the estimated number over all the
bands. If you look at the next page of output (the goodness-of-fit tests)
you can see the actual numbers observed and expected in each of the bands.

There is a little bit about the outputs in the online manual under "Brief
Analysis Guidelines", but I should probably put more explanations about the
plots in there in the next version.

Hope this helps,

- Len Thomas

--

messages.author: 5a0e2c6a2966f877
messages.subject: zero values analyzed as 4th species
parts:
Hello Steve Buckland and Distance users,

I am working on finding the density, detection function, and effective
strip width of three species of primates in La Selva National Park,
Costa Rica. It's taken a while to learn the program, but I think I've
gotten as far as I can, so I am writing now in the hopes that any of you
might know the answers to the following questions:

1.) In my observation layer, I am post stratifying by species. I am
including line transect censuses that did not have any sightings.
Distance is treating these no sightings (no matter if they are entered
as "0" or "default") as a fourth species, and I am afraid this is
biasing my results. How can I tell Distance not to analyze zero values
as a forth species?

2.) Results are showing that my f(0), p, and ESW is exactly the same for
all three species, including my zero values (the imaginary fourth
species). Why is this happening, and how can I fix it?

3.) Also, although this question may arise more from my ignorance than
anything else, how can I have a detection probability greater than 1, or
100%? The first histogram bar on Plot three rises to a detection
probability of 1.54. Do I ignore that and just look at my red function
line (which does rise to exactly 1)?

Any help you can offer would be greatly appreciated.

Sincerely,
Genesis Humphrey
